query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, a synergistic protection arises from the altered defect structure (nanocrystalline grain refinement and lattice distortion) that promotes formation of an adherent, self-healing, noble-element enriched passive oxide layer. This layer serves dual functions: it minimizes mechanical damage (by reducing crack initiation during wear) and retards corrosive dissolution by acting as a robust ionic barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline, primarily single-phase HEA (e.g., BCC or FCC) containing elements such as Cr and Mn that are known to form protective, noble-element enriched oxides, along with significant lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to a controlled environment in which it experiences simultaneous abrasive or sliding wear and exposure to a corrosive electrolyte (for example, a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution).
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature as well as moderate elevated temperatures under constant load and sliding conditions, with parallel tests of wear only, corrosion only, and combined wear–corrosion. A matched baseline (e.g., a conventional alloy or a HEA variant with reduced passive oxide–forming elements) is also tested under identical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a strain-induced, protective oxide layer that is enriched in noble elements and intimately bonded to the distorted nanostructure of the HEA.
generation.mechanism: Lattice distortions and sluggish diffusion in HEAs facilitate quick nucleation and renewal of a passivating oxide at the surface, even as wear produces microdamage. This continuous, self-healing layer limits the exposure of the underlying metal to corrosive species and reduces local stress concentrations that would otherwise propagate cracks during mechanical abrasion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear–corrosion conditions, degradation (measured by mass loss, hardness reduction, and microstructural damage) is expected to be significantly lower than in either pure wear or pure corrosion tests, and markedly lower than in the baseline alloy lacking adequate passive oxide formers. The oxide layer should remain adherent and stable, providing dual protection throughout the test duration.
generation.baseline: A conventional alloy (such as stainless steel) or a HEA with an otherwise similar composition but diminished content of key oxide‐forming elements (e.g., lower Cr or Mn levels).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is effective in environments where the conditions allow for formation and stabilization of the passive film (moderate temperatures and not overly aggressive chemistries). It may fail if the temperature is too high (leading to oxide spallation) or if the corrosive medium aggressively dissolves the protective film.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in degradation rates and the relative contributions of wear-induced and corrosion-induced damage remain to be calibrated experimentally. The durability and renewal kinetics of the oxide layer under dynamic conditions also require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tribocorrosion experiments using a tribometer equipped with an electrochemical cell. Test both the HEA and a compositionally matched baseline (with reduced passive oxide–forming elements) under identical sliding wear and corrosive (3.5 wt% NaCl) conditions at controlled temperatures (room temperature and a moderate elevated temperature). Evaluate the formation, integrity, and renewal of the passive oxide layer via surface analysis (SEM, XPS) before and after testing.
measurements: Electrochemical current and potential profiles to assess corrosion rates
Surface morphology and composition via SEM and XPS (to detect the protective oxide film)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not form a stable, adherent oxide layer under wear–corrosion conditions, or if its combined degradation (mass loss, mechanical degradation) is not significantly lower than that of the baseline alloy, then the hypothesized dual mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. At 300 K and 600 K, the ordered lattice structure of the high entropy alloy coating material is basically the same, and thus its hardness is basically the same. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
